What Dr. Poston says to focus on Built from Dr. Brad Poston's Renal II: Chronic Glomerulonephritis and Glomerular Lesions Associated with Systemic Diseases (slides + narration). Objectives: etiologies of ESRD, diabetic nephropathy, lupus nephritis, and myeloma / amyloidosis in the kidney. He stresses that the CRAB criteria are tested on quizzes and Step exams. Practice questions sit at the end of each section; the summary table is last. beyond source = standard teaching I added; corrected = source slip fixed.

1. Chronic GN, CKD Stages and ESRD Causes

  • Most glomerular diseases (except possibly uncomplicated minimal change disease and thin basement membrane disease) can progress to CKD with falling GFR and eventually ESRD.
  • Clinical: hypertension, renal impairment (decreasing GFR), proteinuria, small shrunken kidneys.
  • CKD = kidney damage or eGFR <60 lasting >3 months. Damage = abnormal urinalysis (proteinuria, hematuria) or structural change on imaging (US, CT). Abnormal labs are usually repeated at 3–6 months to confirm.
StageeGFR (mL/min)Description
1>90Kidney damage with normal GFR
260–89Mild reduction
330–59Moderate reduction
415–29Severe reduction
5<15ESRD

Leading causes of new cases (by primary cause)

CauseShare
Diabetes mellitus44% (most common)
Hypertension28%
Glomerulonephritis~8% (third)
  • Patients may also present with progressive CKD and no known antecedent renal disease.
  • Once ESRD is reached, the pathologic findings are similar whatever the cause.
  • Biopsy is often skipped: no definitive diagnostic findings are likely, and a biopsy that won't change management isn't worth doing. These patients are sometimes labeled with a presumptive diagnosis of "chronic glomerulonephritis."

2. Pathology of the End-Stage Kidney

MethodFinding
GrossSmall, shrunken kidneys (~40 g in the slide vs ~150 g normal); granular subcapsular surface; thin cortex (normal ~10 mm); acquired cysts are common
Light microscopyDiffuse global glomerulosclerosis, tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, chronic inflammation. Bowman's capsule is disrupted and glomerular fibrosis merges with interstitial fibrosis, so architecture is hard to make out
IF / EMMay still show features of a specific glomerular disease, but only if enough nonsclerotic glomeruli remain
Gross. Small shrunken kidneys with a granular surface; thin cortex and acquired cysts on cut section.
Light microscopy. Left: sclerosed glomeruli (arrows), tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, inflammation. Right (trichrome): obsolescent glomeruli with no capillary loops; one residual nonsclerotic glomerulus.

3. Diabetic Nephropathy: Clinical Course and Pathogenesis

Diabetes basics

  • Diagnosis: fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL (no calories ≥8 h); OGTT 2-h glucose ≥200 after 75 g (rarely done, inconvenient); HbA1c ≥6.5% (the usual screen).
  • Macrovascular: atherosclerosis. Microvascular: nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy.
  • Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of ESRD in the U.S., but only 30–40% of patients (type 1 or 2) develop it.
  • Early, sustained glycemic control delays or prevents it; controlled blood pressure also slows progression.

Diagnosis: albuminuria

  • Persistent albuminuria on ≥2 occasions at least 3 months apart. Albuminuria = ≥30 mg/day (timed collection) or ≥30 mg/g (spot albumin-to-creatinine ratio, the usual alternative).
Category24-h collectionSpot ACR
Microalbuminuria30–300 mg30–300 mg/g
Macroalbuminuria (overt nephropathy)>300 mg>300 mg/g

Course: proteinuria rises, GFR falls, and hypertension develops if not already present.

Pathogenesis: two arms

  • Metabolic: excess glucose attaches non-enzymatically to proteins, forming advanced glycation end products (AGEs). (HbA1c is the same process on hemoglobin.) Result: thickened GBM and more mesangial matrix.
  • Hemodynamic: afferent arteriole dilated, efferent arteriole constricted → high glomerular pressure, hypertrophy, more surface area → hyperfiltration, which drives glomerulosclerosis.
  • The proximal tubule reabsorbs glucose; once its capacity is exceeded, glucose spills into urine (glycosuria on UA in uncontrolled disease). Glucose reabsorption pulls sodium with it, and he describes this as inappropriate RAAS activation, constricting the efferent arteriole.
Normal vs diabetes (dilated afferent, constricted efferent, increased pressure, protein loss) vs ACE inhibitor / ARB (efferent dilated, pressure down).
Beyond source beyond sourceBecause efferent constriction is angiotensin II-driven, ACE inhibitors / ARBs (the third nephron on his slide) lower intraglomerular pressure and are the standard renoprotective drugs in diabetic nephropathy; SGLT2 inhibitors also protect the kidney. Neither was discussed in the narration.

Four stages (timeline)

StageYearsFeatures
1. Hyperfiltration0–5Clinically silent. GFR rises (>2 SD above normal mean), peaks, then declines. GBM thickening begins
2. Incipient nephropathy5–15Microalbuminuria; GFR often still normal. Diffuse mesangial sclerosis
3. Overt nephropathy15–25Macroalbuminuria (≥300 mg/24 h); GFR declines. Nodular glomerulosclerosis, tubular and vascular changes
4. ESRD25–30End-stage kidney

4. Diabetic Nephropathy: Light Microscopy

Five findings (slide list): GBM thickening, diffuse mesangial sclerosis, nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson), tubular basement membrane thickening, arteriolar hyalinosis. Early changes are subtle.

GBM thickening (inset upper right: normal GBM). Subtle early.
Diffuse mesangial sclerosis (trichrome): diffuse increase in mesangial matrix.
Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodule (nodular glomerulosclerosis). Multiple nodules can be seen.
Tubular basement membrane thickening.
Arteriolar hyalinosis (hyaline arteriolosclerosis): glassy pink thickened arteriole walls.
Diabetes vs aging / hypertensionTBM thickening and arteriolar hyalinosis also occur with aging and hypertension, just less severe. In aging and hypertension hyalinosis involves the afferent arteriole only; in diabetes it involves both afferent and efferent.

5. Lupus Nephritis: Clinical and Classification

SLE

  • Systemic autoimmune disease of multiple organs; many autoantibodies, notably ANAs. Injury is mainly from immune-complex deposition.
  • ACR classification: 4 of 11 criteria.
#ACR criterion
1Malar rash
2Photosensitivity
3Discoid rash
4Oral ulcers
5Nonerosive arthritis
6Pleuritis / pericarditis
7Renal: persistent proteinuria >500 mg/24 h (or 3+) or cellular casts
8Neurologic: seizures or psychosis
9Hematologic: hemolytic anemia, leukopenia (<4000), lymphopenia (<1500) or thrombocytopenia (<100,000)
10ANA positive
11Immunologic: anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith or antiphospholipid antibody
Malar rash over the cheeks and nasal bridge. It spares the nasolabial folds, which get less sun.

Renal manifestations

  • Can look like nephritic or nephrotic syndrome, RPGN, recurrent micro/gross hematuria, CKD, AKI, or hypertension.
  • At least 10% progress to ESRD.

ISN/RPS classification

ClassNameLight microscopy / depositsClinical
IMinimal mesangialNormal LM; mesangial deposits only on IF (± EM)Normal UA, no/minimal proteinuria, normal creatinine
IIMesangial proliferativeMesangial hypercellularity or matrix expansionMicroscopic hematuria and/or proteinuria
IIIFocalSegmental or global capillary loop lesions in <50% of glomeruli; subendothelial depositsHematuria + proteinuria; some HTN, lower GFR, maybe nephrotic
IVDiffuseLoop lesions in >50%; diffuse subendothelial deposits. Most commonOften severe: hematuria, proteinuria with nephrotic syndrome, HTN, reduced GFR
VMembranousLooks like membranous nephropathyNephrotic-range proteinuria
VIAdvanced sclerosingGlobal sclerosis ≥90% of glomeruliUsually ESRD
Slide slip correctedHis Class V line says "subendothelial immune deposits." Membranous change is subepithelial deposits (which is why silver stain shows spikes); subendothelial deposits belong to Class III/IV.

6. Lupus Nephritis: Pathology by Class

Class II mesangial proliferative: mesangial hypercellularity / matrix expansion.
Class III focal: segmental fibrinoid necrosis.
Class IV diffuse: diffuse endocapillary hypercellularity, loop lesions in >50% of glomeruli.
"Full house" IF: granular IgA, IgG, (IgM) and C1q, C3 all positive.
  • IF: nearly every immunoglobulin and complement stain can be positive, the "full house" pattern.
  • Wire loops (LM) = thick, rigid-looking capillary walls from subendothelial deposits, usually in Class IV.
  • EM: subendothelial dense deposits correspond to the wire loops.
Wire loop lesion (LM): the capillary loop periphery looks round and rigid.
EM: subendothelial dense deposits.

Class V

  • Looks identical to membranous nephropathy: thickened capillary walls with irregular outer contours; silver stain shows numerous microspikes.
Class V: thickened capillary walls.
Class V silver stain: microspikes.

7. Plasma Cell Dyscrasias and Multiple Myeloma

  • A clonal plasma cell population that almost always secretes a monoclonal Ig or Ig fragment, and often makes excess light chains too.
  • Multiple myeloma = malignant plasma cell neoplasm. Amyloidosis can arise from other dyscrasias too; it is the result of the monoclonal protein, not its cause.
CRAB (he flags this as a likely exam question)Calcium (hypercalcemia) · Renal insufficiency · Anemia · Bone (lytic lesions)
Left: marrow aspirate with abnormal plasma cells: binucleate forms, prominent nucleoli, cytoplasmic Ig droplets. Right: skull "punched-out" lytic lesions, usually 1–4 cm.

Detecting the monoclonal protein

  • Protein electrophoresis (SPEP): normal gamma region is polyclonal (broad); a monoclonal gammopathy gives a tall narrow spike.
  • Immunofixation characterizes it: parallel strips are incubated with anti-IgG, -IgA, -IgM, anti-kappa, anti-lambda. Their example shows bands in the IgG and kappa lanes = IgG kappa.
SPEP: normal polyclonal pattern vs monoclonal spike.
Immunofixation: patient serum shows IgG and kappa bands.
  • Normal immunoglobulins are suppressed, so patients are prone to infection.

8. Renal Amyloidosis

ALAA
ProteinImmunoglobulin light chain (formerly "primary")Serum amyloid A
Frequency (U.S.)Majority of amyloidosis; kidney is the most frequently involved organUncommon; second most common cause of renal amyloid
SettingOften plasma cell dyscrasia (e.g., myeloma)Reactive to chronic inflammation
Renal presentationNephrotic syndrome, may progress to ESRD

Pathology

  • Gross: kidney usually enlarged; cut surface pale, "waxy."
  • LM (H&E/PAS): amorphous eosinophilic hyaline deposits in the mesangium and/or capillary loops. This is nonspecific, so a special stain is needed.
  • Congo red binds the beta-pleated sheets: orange-red under bright light and apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
  • Typing by IF: stain for light chains. Their example is lambda = AL (lambda) amyloidosis.
Amorphous pink hyaline material expanding the glomerulus.
IF for lambda: glomerular deposits = AL (lambda) amyloid.
Congo red: orange-red deposits (left) and apple-green birefringence in polarized light (right).
Beyond source beyond sourceOn EM amyloid is non-branching fibrils ~8–12 nm; it is Congo-red positive and PAS/silver weak, which separates it from the dense deposits of lupus.

9. Myeloma Kidney: Light Chain Cast Nephropathy

  • Up to 50% of myeloma patients have impaired renal function; up to 10% need dialysis.
  • Monoclonal proteins (usually light chains) damage the tubules (cast nephropathy) and the glomeruli (amyloid).
  • Light chain cast nephropathy is the most common renal lesion and often presents as AKI.
  • Mechanism: excess light chains pass the glomerulus; when they exceed proximal tubule reabsorption they combine with Tamm-Horsfall protein to form casts. Once enough tubules are obstructed, renal function falls.
  • Other contributors: hypercalcemia, infection, hyperuricemia.
  • Confirm by IF (e.g., casts stain for lambda).
Transcript slip correctedThe narration says the tubular damage is caused by amyloid. The tubular lesion is light chain casts, not amyloid; amyloid is the glomerular lesion.
Light chain casts in tubules (H&E).
IF for lambda: staining of casts confirms light chain cast nephropathy.
Beyond source beyond sourceCasts are often fractured with a surrounding giant cell reaction, and urine dipstick (albumin-specific) can be negative despite heavy light-chain excretion.
